I cannot speak for what process the DHS or the TSA use, but what is done in the industry to ensure the person they're transacting with is not on some blacklist (which is mandatory, as per OFAC regulations) is using fuzzy string matching algorithms. Usually it's some variant of measures like the Jaro-Winkler distance [1], which is commonly used to compare names, or phonetic algorithms like Soundex [2], which we know is used by the US government for the census.
Unfortunately, these algorithms tend to work reasonably well for western names but not so much for picking up the subtleties of other languages and cultures, like "islah" (which apparently means "reform") vs. "islam". author: aus_
storyTitle: The Hercules System/370, ESA/390, and z/Architecture Emulator
text:
Mainframer here. Hercules is a pretty amazing piece of software. (Fun fact: One of the main developers, Jay Maynard [1], is also known as the "Tron guy") Unfortunately, Hercules is as close as the average person can get to the platform without working for a corporation that runs z/OS (the modern successor to MVS) or Linux for System z (s390x Linux running on mainframe hardware) in their shop.
The platform has a big image problem. I personally blame IBM for not maintaining relationships with their education customers in the early 80s. The high cost of the hardware drove universities to adopt the new and exciting (ie cheaper) distributed platforms, and thus breeding a generation of distributed-minded graduates never even hearing about the mainframe platform except in history books. I know, because I was one of them.
Now the industry is now facing an exodous of their mainframe experts as most near retirment. The average age is something like 55-60, ready to retire [2]. There just isn't any young, talented mainframers being educated. IBM has realized this, and they've started the "IBM Academic Initative" to partner with schools and incorporate mainframe into their curriculum. It's a start, but the damage is done.
The technology, however, is top notch. The closed-source software/hardware model provides a lot of performance gains over the open source model. z/OS is updated every year and IBM releases new, faster hardware every year. And it's not always more expensive. An EC10 can consolidate several racks of Linux blades into its zVM hypervisor (btw IBM has been doing virtualization for 30+ years) while processing  145,000 credit card transactions per second into a single refrigerator-size machine 24x7x365.
If you are looking for a new career, consider mainframe [3]. It's the backbone of financial, retail and data processing industries. It may not be as glamorous, but it's not going anywhere. And when all that old mainframe talent retires, you can write your own check.

storyTitle: Is it my fault if you can't handle the truth?
text:
I read some Krisnarmurti. We can put a thousand kinds of labels -truthfull ?- on it.
And he is known as a person who constantly talks about seeking the truth.
(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiddu_Krishnamurti)
One of the features that I pay attention to in his speeches is that he always puts reality in a high, inaccessible, -perhaps-mystical place, interacting with people like sitting together in parks and public places instead of communicating with people through publishing articles. And usually starting with "Let's think together" when putting forward an argument. Knowing something, authority - you can examine it if you're curious, he rejected all serious religious titles given to him and abolished the community that brought him to that position-,
I come across many books "How to argue everyone", "How to win every argument". No, reality is not something that can be grasped only by the mind and reinforced with thoughts and arguments, life is a common field of cognition,
develops through asking questions and getting to know oneself.
As he mentioned a lot, all "isms" are like a kind of mental prison. (I'll try to find individual citations if desired). I found rationalism beautiful, despite the ism at the end,
Although I didn't do much research on it, it caught my interest.
On the other hand, the information I don't remember from where I know is: "Reality is something pure and clear as it is, rather than something that changes with arguments as a result of judgment."
Mental arguments under reality and the prevailing assumptions in them only determine the perception of reality in the viewing community.
I don't want to talk about absolute reality anyway, but I use it in a sentence. After that, saying something like "You can't accept the truth" to someone is like an unfortunate, ignorant attack on each side's own reality. The party that sees himself as the one who knows and tells the truth - there are all kinds of it, the one who dictates, the one who legislates, the one who makes religion - actually does not take the humble position required by science.
  may have distanced himself, put himself in a position he would not want. For the other side, the situation is already pathetic. In my own serious discussions, I note that let's not call it reality, please, but a common consensus area. The other party may break away from the common consensus and find itself in an unpleasant place as alienated and excluded.
After that, it would be like living in a dungeon that creates isms, can make people do very bad things when necessary, and at least does not see the sun - real -. I think accepting the truth may be the way to go, with an open desire, a desire for heart, mind, self-knowledge, and actually accepting the truth as one whole.
In my inner reality, in the mental world, what is called reality is consensus. And reality is experienced in a way that is modest, more or less scientific, by living it, being humble, rather than living in life without a serious will to exist and being presented to outsiders saying this is the truth. It's just experienced, knowing is a mental thing, and reality is beyond mere knowledge - yes, I seem to put the concept on a higher ground - it's a single, changeable whole, reinforced by life. In my experience, the situation is often painful because, let alone thinking together, consensus spaces - forums, political consensus spaces, academies, I don't even want to include religions - are like sunless, depressing places, even under the influence of the pathetic human ego.
We can think about all these things together, I don't expect anyone to agree with me, to approve me with their mind, to be told that you are right - this is ego food, it can get me out of my way - but if you want, let's think about this together.
Wouldn't this world we have created be a place to live if we did not have a common area of consensus and conditioning, if we had a constant fear, punishment and reward mechanism, and these methods are no longer obsolete?
Imagine if I'm presenting all I've said by saying this is the truth,
Will this belong to me, I will write my name under it, if I convince you with scientific evidence, mind games, interesting discussion methods,
Ooh we will say, have we reached the truth, will I start to get fat in a position like a great sage and now be more confident - if it is possible to stay - will I start to lead people and will our ground be reality. I don't know, let's think together if you want, but I think at best we would be like a helpless, sunless forest. Without symbiosis - the forest - pure, direct communication, we can turn to humans who worship the gods of their own creation. I think that happiness, peace, joy, compassion, meaning meaning cannot exist in the realm of pure thought and logic.

text:
In the late 1800's there was increasing interest in mysticism and eastern religions in the West. 
One lady, Helena Blavatsky an Ukrainian co-founded a movement called Theosophy which 
made it's way to India and merged with a mish-mash of Indian nationalists and Hindu philosophers around 1880-1890.

As a young boy JD Krishamurthy (born 1895 in south India) was picked by leaders of the Theosophical Society of India as

that people found hard to understand which only increased his popularity among those seeking Eastern mysticism.
[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiddu_Krishnamurti
Like many Indian godmen and spiritual entrepreneurs, JD Krishnamurthy set out for the most lucrative market for his work: California. He spent the rest of his life churning out psychobabble and settled in lovely Ojai valley (having an affair with his best friend's wife).  For a sampling of JDK's profound wisdom you should check out his quotes [3].
Here's a sampling:
“One is never afraid of the unknown; one is afraid of the known coming to an end.”
― Krishnamurti
“Real learning comes about when the competitive spirit has ceased.”
― J. Krishnamurti
“Tradition becomes our security, and when the mind is secure it is in decay.”
― J. Krishnamurti
